name: Retrieval-Grounded Legal Research
title: Retrieval-Grounded Legal Research
answer: Retrieval-grounded legal research is the practice of answering legal questions by first pulling relevant passages from a defined set of sources and then generating a response that cites those passages. The sources can include case law, statutes, regulations, court rules, secondary treatises, and a firm's internal memos. The method is meant to reduce unsupported claims by making every assertion traceable to a document a reader can inspect. It supports tasks such as finding controlling authority, checking how a rule has been applied, comparing jurisdictions, and drafting research summaries. The site's atlas tracks 29 AI case law precedents, a small and fast-changing corpus that illustrates why grounding matters when the law is new.

sections.body: Retrieval-grounded legal research is the practice of answering legal questions by first pulling relevant passages from a defined set of sources and then generating a response that cites those passages. The sources can include case law, statutes, regulations, court rules, secondary treatises, and a firm's internal memos. The method is meant to reduce unsupported claims by making every assertion traceable to a document a reader can inspect. It supports tasks such as finding controlling authority, checking how a rule has been applied, comparing jurisdictions, and drafting research summaries. The site's atlas tracks 29 AI case law precedents, a small and fast-changing corpus that illustrates why grounding matters when the law is new.
sections.heading: Scope

sections.body: The system runs on a document store that holds the source texts and their metadata, plus one or more indexes for retrieval. A common setup pairs a keyword index, such as a search engine, with a vector index built from embeddings of passages. Access controls, versioning, and citation metadata are part of the infrastructure because legal sources change and because some materials are confidential or privileged. The generator model may run in a private cloud or on premises, depending on the sensitivity of the corpus. The infrastructure must also support logging and audit, so that a later reviewer can see what was searched and what was returned.
sections.heading: What it runs on

sections.body: The work begins with a question that is turned into one or more search queries, often with filters for jurisdiction, court, date, or document type. The retriever returns candidate passages from the indexes, and a re-ranking step sorts them by likely relevance to the question. The generator then composes an answer that quotes or cites the selected passages, and a human reviewer checks each citation against the original source. Teams often build a gold set of questions and known answers to measure whether retrieval finds the right authority and whether the generated answer stays faithful to it. Chunking, metadata, and hybrid search are tuned over time because legal language is precise and a missed passage can change the answer.
sections.heading: How the work is done

sections.body: Rights and risk in this area turn on licensing, confidentiality, privilege, and the accuracy of citations. A retrieval system must respect the terms of the databases it indexes, and it must keep privileged or client-confidential material out of unauthorized stores. Provenance matters because a reader needs to know which version of a statute or regulation was retrieved and when. Outputs are not legal advice, and a qualified lawyer remains responsible for verifying the law and for the strategy that follows. Firms also need audit trails to show what was searched, what was retrieved, and what was relied on.
sections.heading: Rights, risk and provenance

sections.body: The direction of travel is toward tighter grounding, better citation checks, and more integration with the tools lawyers already use. Expect more agentic workflows that can plan a research task, retrieve from multiple sources, and assemble a memo with links to authority. Evaluation standards and court rules on AI use are likely to shape what firms will accept in a filing or an internal memo. The site tracks 6940 state AI bills, a sign that regulatory research will keep expanding and that retrieval systems will need to cover many jurisdictions. Provenance and audit trails will become a normal part of the record, not an afterthought.
